1 Samuel — Book introduction (Modern English production candidate)

This book tells us about Eli and the wickedness of his sons, and about Samuel's character and actions.

It then describes Saul's rise to become king of Israel and his misconduct, ending with his death and preparing the way for David's succession.

David was an outstanding picture of Jesus Christ.

His patience, humility, perseverance, and suffering under persecution from both open enemies and false friends provide an example to the church and to every one of its members.

Many events in this book encourage suffering believers to remain faithful, hopeful and patient.

The book also contains useful cautions and solemn warnings.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesElkanah and his family.1–8Hannah's prayer.9–18Samuel, Hannah presents him to the Lord.19–28
Elkanah's household (verses 1–8)

Elkanah continued to worship at the Lord's altar even though his household was divided by unhappy conflict.

When family worship does not bring an end to disagreements, the disagreements must not bring an end to family worship.

It is unkind to reduce our rightful affection for a relative because of some weakness that person cannot overcome and already suffers from.

Doing so would turn God's providence into an excuse for breaking his command to love and would add suffering to someone already afflicted.

It is an ugly disposition to enjoy grieving a person whose spirit is sorrowful or upsetting someone easily distressed.

We should carry one another's burdens, not increase them.

Hannah found the provocation difficult to bear.

People who are easily upset and take injuries too much to heart harm themselves, depriving themselves of many comforts in life and faith.

We should notice the comforts God gives us so that we do not become absorbed in our troubles.

Remember what is for us, not only what is against us.

Hannah prays in distress (verses 9–18)

Hannah prayed with tears.

She trusted that the merciful God knew the grief of her soul.

The Lord permits us not only to ask generally for good things, but to name the particular blessing that we most desire and need.

Hannah prayed quietly; no one heard her words.

This showed that she believed God knows the heart and its desires.

Eli was the high priest and also a judge in Israel.

He misjudged Hannah.

We should not be quick to accuse others of serious wrongdoing when the matter is still uncertain and unproved.

Hannah did not respond by reminding Eli of his own sons' wicked conduct.

When someone judges us unfairly, we should be doubly careful about our words and not answer accusation with accusation.

Hannah simply explained herself.

We should be willing to do the same.

Eli, in turn, was ready to admit his error.

Hannah left with peace of mind.

She had committed her trouble to the Lord in prayer, and Eli had prayed on her behalf.

Prayer brings relief to a heart that trusts God.

It should even soften the face and visible expression of sorrow.

Those who rightly use the privilege of approaching the mercy seat of God, reconciled to us through Jesus Christ, will not remain forever without comfort.

Hannah presents Samuel to the Lord (verses 19–28)

Elkanah's family had a journey to make, with children to bring along.

Even so, they would not set out until they had worshiped God together.

Prayer and provision do not delay a journey.

People who hurry into travel or business without taking time to worship may go forward without God's presence and blessing.

Although Hannah loved worshiping at God's house, she asked to remain at home for a time.

God desires mercy rather than sacrifice.

Those prevented from attending public worship because they must nurse or care for young children may take comfort from her example.

If they perform that work in a faithful spirit, God will graciously receive it as service to him.

When Hannah presented Samuel to the Lord, she gratefully acknowledged that he had answered her prayer.

Everything we give God was first something we asked for and received from him.

Our gifts to him begin as his gifts to us.

Even as a child, Samuel showed genuine devotion.

Young children should be taught to worship God.

Parents should teach them, bring them to worship and encourage them to participate as well as they can.

God will graciously accept their young efforts and teach them to serve him better.
classic_reading:
[1Sam.1.1-1Sam.1.8]
1 Samuel
In this book we have an account of Eli, and the wickedness of his sons; also of Samuel, his character and actions. Then of the advancement of Saul to be the king of Israel, and his ill behaviour, until his death made way for David's succession to the throne, who was an eminent type of Christ. David's patience, modesty, constancy, persecution by open enemies and feigned friends, are a pattern and example to the church, and to every member of it. Many things in this book encourage the faith, hope, and patience of the suffering believer. It contains also many useful cautions and awful warnings.
Chapter 1
Chapter Outline
Elkanah and his family. | (1-8) |
Hannah's prayer. | (9-18) |
Samuel, Hannah presents him to the Lord. | (19-28) |
Verses 1-8
Elkanah kept up his attendance at God's altar, notwithstanding the unhappy differences in his family. If the devotions of a family prevail not to put an end to its divisions, yet let not the divisions put a stop to the devotions. To abate our just love to any relation for the sake of any infirmity which they cannot help, and which is their affliction, is to make God's providence quarrel with his precept, and very unkindly to add affliction to the afflicted. It is evidence of a base disposition, to delight in grieving those who are of a sorrowful spirit, and in putting those out of humour who are apt to fret and be uneasy. We ought to bear one another's burdens, not add to them. Hannah could not bear the provocation. Those who are of a fretful spirit, and are apt to lay provocations too much to heart, are enemies to themselves, and strip themselves of many comforts both of life and godliness. We ought to notice comforts, to keep us from grieving for crosses. We should look at that which is for us, as well as what is against us.
[1Sam.1.9-1Sam.1.18]
Verses 9-18
Hannah mingled tears with her prayers; she considered the mercy of our God, who knows the troubled soul. God gives us leave, in prayer, not only to ask good things in general, but to mention that special good thing we most need and desire. She spoke softly, none could hear her. Hereby she testified her belief of God's knowledge of the heart and its desires. Eli was high priest, and judge in Israel. It ill becomes us to be rash and hasty in censures of others, and to think people guilty of bad things while the matter is doubtful and unproved. Hannah did not retort the charge, and upbraid Eli with the wicked conduct of his own sons. When we are at any time unjustly censured, we have need to set a double watch before the door of our lips, that we do not return censure for censure. Hannah thought it enough to clear herself, and so must we. Eli was willing to acknowledge his mistake. Hannah went away with satisfaction of mind. She had herself by prayer committed her case to God, and Eli had prayed for her. Prayer is heart's ease to a gracious soul. Prayer will smooth the countenance; it should do so. None will long remain miserable, who use aright the privilege of going to the mercy-seat of a reconciled God in Christ Jesus.
[1Sam.1.19-1Sam.1.28]
Verses 19-28
Elkanah and his family had a journey before them, and a family of children to take with them, yet they would not move till they had worshipped God together. Prayer and provender do not hinder a journey. When men are in such haste to set out upon journeys, or to engage in business, that they have not time to worship God, they are likely to proceed without his presence and blessing. Hannah, though she felt a warm regard for the courts of God's house, begged to stay at home. God will have mercy, and not sacrifice. Those who are detained from public ordinances, by the nursing and tending of little children, may take comfort from this instance, and believe, that if they do that duty in a right spirit, God will graciously accept them therein. Hannah presented her child to the Lord with a grateful acknowledgment of his goodness in answer to prayer. Whatever we give to God, it is what we have first asked and received from him. All our gifts to him were first his gifts to us. The child Samuel early showed true piety. Little children should be taught to worship God when very young. Their parents should teach them in it, bring them to it, and put them on doing it as well as they can; God will graciously accept them, and will teach them to do better.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesHannah's song of thanksgiving.1–10The wickedness of Eli's sons, Samuel's ministry.11–26The prophecy against Eli's family.27–36
Hannah praises the Lord (verses 1–10)

Hannah's heart rejoiced not chiefly in her son Samuel, but in the Lord.

She looked beyond the gift and praised the One who had given it.

She rejoiced in God's salvation and looked ahead to the coming of the One who is the complete salvation of his people.

God can weaken the strong and strengthen the weak whenever he chooses.

If we are poor, the Lord has allowed our poverty; this should encourage contentment with our circumstances.

If we are rich, he has provided our wealth; this should encourage gratitude, cheerful service and generosity toward others.

God is not impressed by worldly wisdom or the qualities people boast about.

He chooses those whom the world considers foolish, teaches them their guilt and helps them recognize the priceless value of his freely given salvation.

Hannah's prophecy looks forward to the kingdom of Christ.

After describing the Lord's rule over his providential world, she speaks of his kingdom of grace.

Here Henry identifies the first appearance of the title “Messiah,” or “Anointed.”

Those who belong to Christ's kingdom will be kept safe.

Its enemies will be ruined.

The Anointed One, the Lord Jesus Christ, has power both to save and to judge.

Eli's sons act wickedly; Samuel serves faithfully (verses 11–26)

Samuel had been set apart for God's service in a special way.

From childhood he performed the sanctuary duties appropriate to his ability.

Because his heart was devoted to God, Scripture describes even those simple tasks as ministering to the Lord.

The Lord blessed him.

Young people who serve God as faithfully as they can will be helped to improve and serve him still better.

Eli, however, avoided inconvenience and exertion.

He indulged his children instead of using parental authority to restrain and correct them while they were young.

He overlooked abuses at the sanctuary until they became established habits and led to serious wrongdoing.

His sons should have been teaching worshipers what was good.

Instead, they encouraged them toward evil.

Their wrongdoing happened even in the setting of sacrifices for sin, which pictured the Savior's atonement.

To sin against the very provision for atonement is especially dangerous.

It amounts to trampling the blood of the covenant underfoot.

Eli's rebuke was much too weak and gentle.

Children brought up in godly households may become especially corrupt if they break through every restraint.

A prophecy announces judgment on Eli's household (verses 27–36)

Parents who knowingly allow children to continue in wrongdoing and make no proper effort to restrain them are effectively honoring their children more than God.

Eli's example should move parents to oppose the first signs of wickedness and raise children in the Lord's teaching and correction.

Yet amid the judgment pronounced on Eli's house, God promised mercy to Israel.

His work will not fail because there are no servants available to carry it out.

Jesus Christ is the merciful and faithful High Priest whom God raised up when the Levitical priesthood gave way.

He perfectly performed his Father's will.

God will build him a lasting house, founded securely on a rock, against which hell itself cannot prevail.
classic_reading:
[1Sam.2.1-1Sam.2.10]
Chapter 2
Chapter Outline
Hannah's song of thanksgiving. | (1-10) |
The wickedness of Eli's sons, Samuel's ministry. | (11-26) |
The prophecy against Eli's family. | (27-36) |
Verses 1-10
Hannah's heart rejoiced, not in Samuel, but in the Lord. She looks beyond the gift, and praises the Giver. She rejoiced in the salvation of the Lord, and in expectation of His coming, who is the whole salvation of his people. The strong are soon weakened, and the weak are soon strengthened, when God pleases. Are we poor? God made us poor, which is a good reason why we should be content, and make up our minds to our condition. Are we rich? God made us rich, which is a good reason why we should be thankful, and serve him cheerfully, and do good with the abundance he gives us. He respects not man's wisdom or fancied excellences, but chooses those whom the world accounts foolish, teaching them to feel their guilt, and to value his free and precious salvation. This prophecy looks to the kingdom of Christ, that kingdom of grace, of which Hannah speaks, after having spoken largely of the kingdom of providence. And here is the first time that we meet with the name MESSIAH, or his Anointed. The subjects of Christ's kingdom will be safe, and the enemies of it will be ruined; for the Anointed, the Lord Christ, is able to save, and to destroy.
[1Sam.2.11-1Sam.2.26]
Verses 11-26
Samuel, being devoted to the Lord in a special manner, was from a child employed about the sanctuary in the services he was capable of. As he did this with a pious disposition of mind, it was called ministering unto the Lord. He received a blessing from the Lord. Those young people who serve God as well as they can, he will enable to improve, that they may serve him better. Eli shunned trouble and exertion. This led him to indulge his children, without using parental authority to restrain and correct them when young. He winked at the abuses in the service of the sanctuary till they became customs, and led to abominations; and his sons, who should have taught those that engaged in the service of the sanctuary what was good, solicited them to wickedness. Their offence was committed even in offering the sacrifices for sins, which typified the atonement of the Saviour! Sins against the remedy, the atonement itself, are most dangerous, they tread under foot the blood of the covenant. Eli's reproof was far too mild and gentle. In general, none are more abandoned than the degenerate children of godly persons, when they break through restraints.
[1Sam.2.27-1Sam.2.36]
Verses 27-36
Those who allow their children in any evil way, and do not use their authority to restrain and punish them, in effect honour them more than God. Let Eli's example excite parents earnestly to strive against the beginnings of wickedness, and to train up their children in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. In the midst of the sentence against the house of Eli, mercy is promised to Israel. God's work shall never fall to the ground for want of hands to carry it on. Christ is that merciful and faithful High Priest, whom God raised up when the Levitical priesthood was thrown off, who in all things did his Father's mind, and for whom God will build a sure house, build it on a rock, so that hell cannot prevail against it.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe word of the Lord first revealed to Samuel.1–10God tells Samuel the destruction of Eli's house.11–18Samuel established to be a prophet.19–21
God calls the young Samuel (verses 1–10)

When divine grace intends that a call should be effective, the Lord will repeat the call until the person responds.

Eli realized that Samuel was hearing the Lord's voice and taught him how to answer.

It was a humbling matter for Eli that God addressed Samuel rather than him.

Nevertheless, he helped the younger boy understand what to do.

Older believers should do everything they can to support and improve the abilities of younger people who are coming after them.

We should not withhold help even from people who may soon be given a higher position than our own (John 1:30).

Children should learn good words and responses while they are young, so that they become prepared to learn spiritual truth and take it seriously.

Samuel hears judgment against Eli's house (verses 11–18)

How much guilt and corruption remains in us!

We are often aware of sins that our own hearts know well.

People who have the responsibility and power to restrain others from wrongdoing, yet refuse to act, share in that guilt.

They will be accountable as participants in the wrong.

Eli's response to the fearful sentence showed that he recognized God's right to act as he saw fit.

He trusted the Lord would do nothing unjust.

The gentleness, patience and humility of Eli's words show genuine repentance.

He accepted the consequences of his own failure.

Samuel grows as God's prophet (verses 19–21)

Every increase in wisdom and grace comes from God being with us.

The Lord graciously continues his visits to those who receive them rightly.

Early faith is a young person's greatest honor.

Those who honor God will be honored by him.

Young people should consider Samuel's example and remember their Creator during their youth.

Even small children are capable of genuine faith.

Samuel shows that their worship and trust can please the Lord.

His gentle and beautiful qualities of character are the brightest adornment of youth and a sure source of true happiness.
classic_reading:
[1Sam.3.1-1Sam.3.10]
Chapter 3
Chapter Outline
The word of the Lord first revealed to Samuel. | (1-10) |
God tells Samuel the destruction of Eli's house. | (11-18) |
Samuel established to be a prophet. | (19-21) |
Verses 1-10
The call which Divine grace designs shall be made effectual; will be repeated till it is so, till we come to the call. Eli, perceiving that it was the voice of God that Samuel heard, instructed him what to say. Though it was a disgrace to Eli, for God's call to be directed to Samuel, yet he told him how to meet it. Thus the elder should do their utmost to assist and improve the younger that are rising up. Let us never fail to teach those who are coming after us, even such as will soon be preferred before us, [John.1.30] Joh 1:30. Good words should be put into children's mouths betimes, by which they may be prepared to learn Divine things, and be trained up to regard them.
[1Sam.3.11-1Sam.3.18]
Verses 11-18
What a great deal of guilt and corruption is there in us, concerning which we may say, It is the iniquity which our own heart knoweth; we are conscious to ourselves of it! Those who do not restrain the sins of others, when it is in their power to do it, make themselves partakers of the guilt, and will be charged as joining in it. In his remarkable answer to this awful sentence, Eli acknowledged that the Lord had a right to do as he saw good, being assured that he would do nothing wrong. The meekness, patience, and humility contained in those words, show that he was truly repentant; he accepted the punishment of his sin.
[1Sam.3.19-1Sam.3.21]
Verses 19-21
All increase in wisdom and grace, is owing to the presence of God with us. God will graciously repeat his visits to those who receive them aright. Early piety will be the greatest honour of young people. Those who honour God he will honour. Let young people consider the piety of Samuel, and from him they will learn to remember their Creator in the days of their youth. Young children are capable of religion. Samuel is a proof that their waiting upon the Lord will be pleasing to him. He is a pattern of all those amiable tempers, which are the brightest ornament of youth, and a sure source of happiness.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe Israelites overcome by the Philistines.1–9The ark taken.10, 11The death of Eli.12–18The birth of Ichabod.19–22
Israel is defeated by the Philistines (verses 1–9)

Israel was defeated because sin—the accursed thing—remained in its camp, giving its enemies every advantage they needed.

The people recognized that God had allowed their trouble.

But instead of submitting, they complained angrily, as though they had done nothing to provoke him.

A person's own foolishness spoils the way, and then the heart becomes angry with the Lord (Proverbs 19:3), finding fault with him.

Israel supposed that bringing the ark into camp would force God to appear and fight for them.

People who have declined spiritually can sometimes become extremely attached to outward religious observances, imagining that these will save them.

The ark represented God's throne.

But bringing that throne into a military camp could not bring anyone to heaven while the world and the flesh ruled the heart.

The ark is captured (verses 10 and 11)

The Philistines took the ark.

This was a terrible judgment on Israel and a sure sign of God's displeasure.

Let no one imagine that an outward profession of religion can shelter a person from God's wrath.

Eli dies (verses 12–18)

The army's defeat grieved Eli deeply as a judge of Israel.

As a father, he also suffered when he learned that his two sons had died—the very sons he had treated with such indulgence, and who, he had reason to fear, died without repentance.

But the greatest blow came when the messenger announced that the ark of God had been taken.

That news struck Eli to the heart, and he died at once.

A person can die in terrible circumstances without necessarily being lost eternally.

Someone may experience an untimely and distressing death yet have peace with God in the end.

Ichabod is born (verses 19–22)

The wife of Phinehas appears to have been a godly woman.

As she was dying, she grieved most over the ark being captured and God's glory departing from Israel.

What value could earthly happiness have for someone who was facing death?

At that moment, only joy that is spiritual and divine can truly comfort.

And how can people enjoy the comforts of creation when they have lost God's word and appointed worship—especially when they no longer enjoy the blessing of his gracious presence and the light of his face?

If God departs, the glory departs, and with it all that is truly good.

Woe to us if he leaves!

Yet even when God's glory is withdrawn from one sinful nation, town or village after another, it never disappears from the earth altogether.

When his light is hidden in one place, he causes it to shine somewhere else.

[1Sam.4.1-1Sam.4.9]
Chapter 4
Chapter Outline
The Israelites overcome by the Philistines. | (1-9) |
The ark taken. | (10-11) |
The death of Eli. | (12-18) |
The birth of Ichabod. | (19-22) |
Verses 1-9
Israel is smitten before the Philistines. Sin, the accursed thing, was in the camp, and gave their enemies all the advantage they could wish for. They own the hand of God in their trouble; but, instead of submitting, they speak angrily, as not aware of any just provocation they had given him. The foolishness of man perverts his way, and then his heart frets against the Lord, [Prov.19.3] Pr 19:3, and finds fault with him. They supposed that they could oblige God to appear for them, by bringing the ark into their camp. Those who have gone back in the life of religion, sometimes discover great fondness for the outward observances of it, as if those would save them; and as if the ark, God's throne, in the camp, would bring them to heaven, though the world and the flesh are on the throne in the heart.
[1Sam.4.10-1Sam.4.11]
Verses 10-11
The taking of the ark was a great judgment upon Israel, and a certain token of God's displeasure. Let none think to shelter themselves from the wrath of God, under the cloak of outward profession.
[1Sam.4.12-1Sam.4.18]
Verses 12-18
The defeat of the army was very grievous to Eli as a judge; the tidings of the death of his two sons, to whom he had been so indulgent, and who, as he had reason to fear, died impenitent, touched him as a father; yet there was a greater concern on his spirit. And when the messenger concluded his story with, "The ark of God is taken," he is struck to the heart, and died immediately. A man may die miserably, yet not die eternally; may come to an untimely end, yet the end be peace.
[1Sam.4.19-1Sam.4.22]
Verses 19-22
The wife of Phinehas seems to have been a person of piety. Her dying regret was for the loss of the ark, and the departure of the glory from Israel. What is any earthly joy to her that feels herself dying? No joy but that which is spiritual and divine, will stand in any stead then; death is too serious a thing to admit the relish of any earthly joy. What is it to one that is lamenting the loss of the ark? What pleasure can we take in our creature comforts and enjoyments, if we want God's word and ordinances; especially if we want the comfort of his gracious presence, and the light of his countenance? If God go, the glory goes, and all good goes. Woe unto us if he depart! But though the glory is withdrawn from one sinful nation, city, or village after another, yet it shall never depart altogether, but shines forth in one place when eclipsed in another.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesDagon is broken before the ark.1–5The Philistine smitten.6–12
Dagon falls before the ark (verses 1–5)

See how the ark of God triumphed over Dagon.

In the same way, Satan's kingdom will surely fall before Christ's kingdom.

Error will give way to truth, irreverence to godliness, and sinful corruption to grace within believers' hearts.

Even when true religion seems close to defeat, we can remain confident that its victory will come.

When Christ, the true Ark of the covenant, enters a fallen human heart, he enters what had been Satan's temple.

Then the idols fall.

Every attempt to restore them is vain.

Sin is abandoned, unjust gain restored and the Lord takes his rightful place upon the throne.

Yet pride, self-love and worldly desires, although overthrown and crucified, still remain within us like Dagon's broken stump.

We must watch and pray that they do not regain power.

Let us seek the more complete destruction of every lingering sin.

God's judgment falls on the Philistines (verses 6–12)

The Lord's hand was heavy upon the Philistines.

He not only demonstrated the folly of their idol worship but severely corrected their insolence.

Still they would not abandon Dagon.

Rather than seek God's mercy, they tried to remove his ark.

People whose hearts are ruled by worldly desires may suffer under God's judgments and still prefer to push him away instead of entering fellowship with him and seeking his friendship.

But every plan they made to escape God's judgment only increased their suffering.

Anyone who insists on fighting against God will soon discover the cost.
classic_reading:
[1Sam.5.1-1Sam.5.5]
Chapter 5
Chapter Outline
Dagon is broken before the ark. | (1-5) |
The Philistine smitten. | (6-12) |
Verses 1-5
See the ark's triumph over Dagon. Thus the kingdom of Satan will certainly fall before the kingdom of Christ, error before truth, profaneness before godliness, and corruption before grace in the hearts of the faithful. When the interests of religion seem to be ready to sink, even then we may be confident that the day of their triumph will come. When Christ, the true Ark of the covenant, really enters the heart of fallen man, which is indeed Satan's temple, all idols will fall, every endeavour to set them up again will be vain, sin will be forsaken, and unrighteous gain restored; the Lord will claim and possess the throne. But pride, self-love, and worldly lusts, though dethroned and crucified, still remain within us, like the stump of Dagon. Let us watch and pray that they may not prevail. Let us seek to have them more entirely destroyed.
[1Sam.5.6-1Sam.5.12]
Verses 6-12
The hand of the Lord was heavy upon the Philistines; he not only convinced them of their folly, but severely chastised their insolence. Yet they would not renounce Dagon; and instead of seeking God's mercy, they desired to get clear of his ark. Carnal hearts, when they smart under the judgments of God, would rather, if it were possible, put him far from them, than enter into covenant or communion with him, and seek him for their friend. But their devices to escape the Divine judgments only increase them. Those that fight against God will soon have enough of it.

modern_osis:
Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe Philistines consult how to send back the ark.1–9They bring it to Bethshemesh.10–18The people smitten for looking into the ark.19–21
The Philistines prepare to return the ark (verses 1–9)

The Philistines endured punishment for seven months while the ark remained among them.

They prolonged their own misery because they refused to send it away sooner.

Sinners often do the same when they will not part with their sins.

The Israelites themselves made no effort to recover the ark.

How rarely concern for true religion outweighs other concerns!

In a time of public disaster, people fear for themselves, their families and their nation.

But who is concerned for God's ark?

We have been granted the gospel, yet it is often neglected or despised.

We should not be surprised if that privilege is removed.

For many people, even the loss of the gospel—one of the gravest possible judgments—would bring no sadness.

They would be as satisfied with almost any religious profession as with Christianity.

But other people prize God's house, word and ministry more highly than their greatest possessions.

They dread losing these blessings even more than death.

Ungodly people are eager to avoid the conviction of their own consciences.

When trouble comes, they insist it is merely chance rather than acknowledging a warning from God.

The ark comes to Beth-shemesh (verses 10–18)

The two cows recognized their great Owner—the Lord—whom Hophni and Phinehas had failed to recognize rightly.

God's providence attends even to animals and makes use of them for his purposes.

When the harvesters saw the ark return, they rejoiced.

Their joy over the ark was greater than their joy over the harvest.

When public worship and God's appointed ordinances return after persecution or trouble, there is good reason for great rejoicing.

Judgment follows irreverent curiosity (verses 19–21)

People seriously offend God when they pry into secret matters that do not belong to them (Deuteronomy 29:29; Colossians 2:18).

Humanity's ruin began with the desire for forbidden knowledge.

The Lord will not allow his ark to be treated irreverently.

God cannot be mocked.

Those who refuse to revere his goodness or receive his gracious gifts with respect may be made to experience his justice.

Henry notes that the number of people killed is expressed unusually in the original text, and he considers 1,170 a probable interpretation.

This is his textual estimate—not a change to the biblical text or a claim about the exact numbering of any modern Bible edition.

The people now wanted the ark removed.

What foolishness, to run from one extreme to another!

Instead of demanding that the ark leave, they should have asked, “How may we be reconciled to God and recover his favor?” (Micah 6:6–7).

Similarly, when God's word awakens terror in a sinner's conscience, some refuse to accept their own guilt.

They quarrel with Scripture and push it away.

Many suppress their convictions and thereby reject the salvation offered to them.
classic_reading:
[1Sam.6.1-1Sam.6.9]
Chapter 6
Chapter Outline
The Philistines consult how to send back the ark. | (1-9) |
They bring it to Bethshemesh. | (10-18) |
The people smitten for looking into the ark. | (19-21) |
Verses 1-9
Seven months the Philistines were punished with the presence of the ark; so long it was a plague to them, because they would not send it home sooner. Sinners lengthen out their own miseries by refusing to part with their sins. The Israelites made no effort to recover the ark. Alas! where shall we find concern for religion prevail above all other matters? In times of public calamity we fear for ourselves, for our families, and for our country; but who cares for the ark of God? God's law and ordinary human conduct differ greatly.

God's law should govern how we treat others.

But what people usually do may teach us what disappointments to expect from them.

Israel would complain under the new system, but God would not immediately answer those complaints.
